title: The good room
summary: Millions of people have visited Lascaux. Almost none of them have been to Lascaux. An opinion episode on copies that are better than the original, AI answers that arrive too complete, and the discipline of letting a gap stay a gap.
music: Quiet contemplative piano and cello theme for an essay podcast, warm and spacious, no vocals.

sources.name: Pew Research Center, AI summaries and clicks (July 2025)

lines: This is After the Headline, from AI Broadsheet. I'm Jack. This one's an opinion episode, our newsroom's view, labelled as such.
I'm Nora. And it starts in a hole in the ground in south-western France.
September twelfth, nineteen forty. Four teenagers climb down into a cave near Montignac and find a room with animals on the walls. Horses, stags, aurochs. Painted around twenty thousand years ago.

Lascaux. It opened to the public in nineteen forty-eight, and it did what any wonder does. It drew crowds. And the crowds changed it. Breath, heat, humidity, electric light. Algae on the walls, then mineral deposits.
Looking at the paintings was destroying the paintings. So in nineteen sixty-three, France closed it.
And built a copy. Lascaux Two in nineteen eighty-three. Then a far more complete facsimile, Lascaux Four, opened in December twenty sixteen, built from millimetre-scale scans.
And here's the uncomfortable part. The copy is very good. Better lit than the original ever was. No queues damaging anything. You can stand in front of one horse for as long as you like.
By almost every measure, it's better. And it's honest. Nobody pretends the replica is the cave.
So millions of people have been to Lascaux. And almost none of them have been to Lascaux.
The original is still there. In the dark, a short walk away, monitored constantly. Watched very closely and hardly ever entered. And that's the right decision.
That's the shape we want to talk about. Not a lie. Not a loss. A copy so good, so available, so comfortable, that nobody walks toward the original anymore. And nobody decided it.

Which brings us to now. In July twenty twenty-five, Pew Research looked at how people used Google. When an AI summary appeared at the top, people clicked a regular search result in eight percent of visits. Without the summary, fifteen percent.
And the source links inside the AI summary itself? Clicked in about one percent of visits.
One percent. The summary is the replica. The source is the cave.
And again, the summary is often good. That's the point. This isn't a story about bad technology.

Here's another way in. Nobody knows, in any settled sense, what the Lascaux paintings were for. Serious scholars disagree. There's a famous scene deep in the cave, a figure with a bird's head, a bison, a bird on a stick, that's been interpreted again and again and is still unsettled.
The honest answer is: we don't know.

But you can now ask a machine, and get a fluent, well-sourced, confident account of what it means. Not a lie. Just complete. Without the hesitations and the competing readings that a specialist would include.
Because those hesitations are what specialists say when they don't know.
So the reader walks away satisfied, holding an answer to a question that doesn't have one.

This is our view, and it's a small one. The skill this period is most likely to lose is knowing when a gap should stay a gap. Saying I'm not sure. A teacher saying it in front of a class. An editor asking: how do you know that?
Nobody sells that. There's no industry behind an unanswered question.
And there's a fear underneath all this, and it deserves a straight answer. People aren't really afraid that machines will be smarter. They're afraid of being unnecessary.
And that fear isn't about machines. It's about what our societies do with people they decide they no longer need. That was here before AI.
Which is the better news. Nobody controls what the next model can do. But arrangements are made by people. In rooms. On Tuesdays.
Whether a clinic keeps time for someone to sit down. Whether a school protects the years when a person is formed, not just informed. Those are decisions.
So use the good room. It's a very good room. Just remember the cave is still there. And sometimes, walk toward it.
That's After the Headline. Our reporting, the sources and The Sir Jack Files are at AI Broadsheet dot com.
